cards.title: The Delicate Dance: Keep Supply Under Demand
cards.summary: Manage the ratio of satisfied desire to unmet desire so demand stays ravenous and each launch sells out.
cards.use_when: Planning recurring promotions, cohort launches or high-ticket services, and deciding how many units or spots to release.
steps: Recognize that demand is fractal (80/20-shaped), not linear: roughly one fifth of prospects may be willing to pay five times the price or more. A group of ten at $500 may include two willing to pay $5,000 — selling fewer units at the higher price can mean more profit, more value delivered and less cost.
Deliberately leave desire unsatisfied: cap supply below what you could sell, so buyers who miss out carry pent-up desire into the next launch and act with more urgency.

Expect compounding effects on the next promotion: onlookers who see sold-out status and happy buyers want in more, and new prospects outside the original pool enter. Example sequence: open three spots at the higher price after selling out the previous round and fill them — still leaving unmet demand.

Avoid the opposite trap: re-promoting a fully-satisfied offer (e.g. the $500 tier everyone already bought) typically sells fewer slots each time, eventually drying up. The source frames this as the root of businesses constantly scrambling for fresh demand.
Internalize the stated principle: "The longer you delay the ask, the bigger the ask you can make" — a longer runway allows a bigger plane to take off.
Balance the extremes: zero supply earns nothing and eventually feels like rejection (and takes longer than you expect for people to leave); satisfying all demand kills the golden goose.
caveats: This is the source's framing ('demand is fractal'), not a measured law; treat the 20%/5x ratio as an illustrative pattern.
Under-supplying is a long-game strategy — it deliberately forgoes near-term revenue.
The source notes people tolerate rejection from a brand far longer than most owners assume, but this is his experience, not a guarantee.

cards.title: How Premium Prices Are Actually Made: Scarcity of Solvers
cards.summary: Price power comes from buyers perceiving very few people who can solve their specialized problem, combined with the value of the outcome.
cards.use_when: Positioning high-ticket services or coaching, or explaining to a client why cheaper competitors are not real alternatives.
steps: Diagnose the buyer's situation: if the problem is rare and blocks their happiness, it consumes their attention; the more specialized the problem, the fewer available solvers. In extreme cases the buyer perceives supply = 1.

Compare problem specificity: many people can teach 'how to make $10,000/month'; far fewer can address 'how to add $5M in profit without adding product lines' — the source cites a real project he solved in 60 minutes by slightly altering a pricing model.

Factor in time-to-outcome: if a solution accelerates a goal by one or two years, or immediately yields hundreds of thousands or millions, its perceived value rises sharply. Paying $50,000 for a day that adds $500,000/month in revenue within three months is framed as an obvious ROI.

Accept that value and rarity compound: the client is paying for accumulated expertise and to skip the cost and time of errors — going straight to the good stuff faster and cheaper than figuring it out alone.

Note the leverage of not needing the sale: the source declined two $50,000/day offers because his business already made more per day. The side that needs the exchange less has the upper hand — a pricing and negotiation principle he says has served him best.
caveats: The $50,000/day and $5M examples are the author's personal case studies, not benchmarks for other businesses.
Perceived scarcity can be implied by authority or fame, but manufacturing a false supply=1 claim is misrepresentation.
High-ticket day rates depend on the buyer's economics; a $500k/month revenue lift is not a typical or promised outcome.

cards.title: Creating Scarcity with Limited Releases and Public Sellouts
cards.summary: Cap physical product runs, sell out consistently, and broadcast the sellout to compound desire over time.
cards.use_when: Running limited-edition or seasonal product drops for a physical-goods ecommerce brand.
steps: Pick the axis of limitation: flavor, color, design, size or quantity — e.g. 'this month we release 100 boxes of mint chocolate cookie protein bars.'
Deliberately make fewer than you believe you can sell, so you reliably sell out. The source states it is better to sell out consistently than to over-order and fail to create scarcity.

Announce the sellout publicly. Fence-sitters see social proof that others judged it worth buying, and the decision is taken away from them — which increases desire and makes them far more likely to buy the next drop.
Repeat on a cadence, but not too often: roughly once a month is the sweet spot among companies the source knows that do this regularly.

Study Chanel as the reference model: sending only one to two of each piece per store means every store carries a different selection and each item is the last or second-to-last in stock, supporting margins far above market over a century.
caveats: This is a compounding strategy only if you actually sell out — a failed 'limited' run undercuts credibility.
Overusing drops dilutes the effect; the source warns against too-frequent releases.
The Chanel analogy is a brand observation, not a replicable tactic for every business.

cards.title: Four Ethical Scarcity Structures for Services
cards.summary: Use total-cap, weekly-cap, cohort-cap or no-reentry scarcity to raise take rates on service offers without being phony.
cards.use_when: Selling ongoing services, agency retainers or high-touch tiers where a fixed quantity of clients is genuinely serviceable.
steps: Total business cap: publicly commit to accepting X clients total at a service level, maintain a waiting list, and let prospects jump in the moment a door opens — the source reports price resistance disappears. Periodically raise capacity by 10–20% and re-cap, or raise prices and squeeze out lower-performing accounts.

Growth rate cap: state how many new clients you accept per week and how many spots remain, e.g. 'we take 5 per week, 3 are taken, I have 6 more calls this week.' This works because you genuinely can only onboard so many at once.

Cohort cap: accept X clients per class or cohort on whatever cadence you choose — monthly, quarterly or four times a year. 'We take 100 clients 4 times a year; doors open then close.' This also creates operational cadence for onboarding.

Use scarcity for higher-ticket upsells: workshops, trainings, events, seminars and consulting naturally take time and grant access, so fixed seats or spots rapidly drive demand. Always have fewer spots than you think you can sell so the sellout is remembered.

Honest scarcity is the most ethical version: define a number you are genuinely willing to take on, then advertise it. Telling people you are 81% to capacity or three-quarters full for the week moves fence-sitters, and capacity itself implies social proof.
caveats: The source insists these only work ethically when the limit is real, or when it is a limit you define and honour.
Waiting-list and re-cap mechanics require disciplined delivery capacity.
Cohort cadence is more powerful the less frequently you start clients, but slower cadences defer revenue.

cards.title: Extreme Scarcity: Selling Capped 1-on-1 Access
cards.summary: Create a very high-priced, tightly capped access tier to a person and announce it, for outsized short-term revenue.
cards.use_when: Designing a premium tier, advisory or VIP access level where a founder's personal time is the product.
steps: Choose the access medium that fits how you actually like working — direct messages, email, phone, voice memos, Zoom calls. The source hates email and messages but does not mind Zoom, so he limits delivery to what he does not resent.
Cap the tier at a tiny number of clients and price it very high, then tell people it exists.
Keep delivery unscalable on purpose: the source says this is the fastest way he knows to make a lot of money, and that these tend to be some of the best clients.

Consider a no-reentry rule — once a client leaves the capped level, they can never return. He first used this with his gyms, then in a mastermind, then in a higher level of Gym Lords. It works best with small groups and loses teeth as groups get much bigger.
Accept that the '1% of 1%' of prospects will adjust and take action — you are not trying to convert everyone.
caveats: The source explicitly calls this unscalable and says the pricing can exceed what you thought possible — treat as a strategy for a narrow tier, not the whole business.
He does not recommend it for people who hate money's counterpart: the delivery burden of personal access.
No-reentry clauses weaken as the group scales up.

cards.title: Urgency Basics: Deadlines Drive Decisions
cards.summary: Scarcity limits quantity; urgency limits time — a defined cutoff creates action without changing the offer.
cards.use_when: Adding a time-based mechanism to a launch, promotion or sales conversation that currently has no deadline.
steps: Separate the two levers: scarcity is a function of quantity; urgency is a function of time. Use them together often, but design them deliberately and separately.
Defined deadlines or cutoffs for purchase create urgency — 'deadlines drive decisions' is the source's stated maxim.
Choose from his four preferred ethical mechanisms: rolling cohorts, rolling seasonal urgency, promotional/pricing urgency, and exploding opportunity.

Expect the effect to concentrate at the end: on week-long campaigns or launches, the biggest sales come in the last four hours of the last day — up to 50–60% of sales in the final 3% of the time allotted, which he calls illogical but unmistakably human.

Do not fear turning away late buyers: the source says the fear of losing sales is unfounded because people who miss the deadline rarely would have bought even with pressure. Satisfy the many who act instead of mourning the few who never would have.
caveats: His 50–60% figure comes from observing launches; treat it as a pattern, not a rule for every campaign.
Fake deadlines destroy credibility — the source is explicit that countdowns must be real.
Category scope note: much of this section is written for services and info products; the ecommerce translation is applying a genuine cutoff to a drop, bundle or promotion.

cards.title: Rolling Cohort Urgency for Services and Courses
cards.summary: Start clients on a fixed cadence so every prospect has a reason to buy today instead of waiting a week or a quarter.
cards.use_when: Running an onboarding, course, group program or service with recurring start dates.
steps: Set a regular kickoff cadence — weekly, biweekly, monthly or quarterly — and tell prospects what signing up today means: 'sign up today and you are in Monday's group, otherwise you wait until the next start date.'

Add a small concrete nudge: mention a specific opening from a dropout ('a client from a few weeks ago dropped out, so I have an opening for Monday's cohort; if you are going to do this sooner or later, might as well start now and reap the rewards sooner at the same price').
Recognize the corollary: the less frequently you start clients, the stronger the urgency — twice a year is very powerful as the date approaches; every other week still confers a nudge.

Handle a buyer who wants in right after a cohort started: either (a) offer a speedy personalized onboarding as a sign-up-today bonus to get them in, or (b) his preference — explain the advantages of waiting, such as more time to review materials and talk to employees (B2B) or family (B2C), plus an extended payment plan available only to them because the start date is far out.
Remember who controls the cadence: 'you always have the advantage because you are the one who calls the shots.'
Treat cohort cadence as operational infrastructure too — it forces a choreographed onboarding experience that matters more as you scale.
caveats: Longer gaps between starts create stronger urgency but slower cash flow.
The extended-payment-plan and bonus onboarding offers are inducements; only promise terms you will honour.
This is a services/education pattern; ecommerce equivalents are launch windows or scheduled restocks.

cards.title: Seasonal and Promotional Urgency Wrappers
cards.summary: Give the same core offer a dated seasonal name and real deadline so it reads as a limited window.
cards.use_when: Local or ecommerce promotions that need novelty without changing the underlying product or service.
steps: Put the real promotion dates on landing pages and in copy, and make them visible everywhere. If the dates are not real, you lose credibility and look like every other wannabe marketer.

Rename the same core promotion by season to create a genuine start and finish: 'New Year Promotion ends Jan 30', 'Valentines Lovers Promo ends Feb 28', 'Sexy By Spring Special ends March 31', 'Fools in Love April Promo ends April 30'.
Fire up a new ad campaign and landing page with new dates when the old one ends — the source says this takes about five minutes of editing and produces a large conversion lift.
For local businesses, use this as the number-one strategy: vary marketing more frequently than national advertisers, since a new dated wrapper on the same core service adds urgency and novelty.

Use pricing/bonus-based urgency instead of a service cutoff when you sell year round: 'let's start today to get the discount you came in for; we change them every four weeks and this is one of the better ones' — the risk is missing the promotion, not the service.
Swap among pricing promotions, discounts, free install, free onboarding or an added workshop (e.g. valued at $1,000) to create urgency around interchangeable parts.
When genuinely raising prices, announce it: 'The price is going up — get in now.' He says never raise prices silently, as it signals strength and flushes fence-sitters out of the pipeline.
caveats: The source warns that fake countdowns cost credibility; the deadline must be enforceable.
Promo/bonus urgency keeps integrity only if you frame it as the promotion ending, not a lie that you will refuse service after the date.
He frames pipeline-clearing price-rise announcements as a cash injection from already-warm leads — do not use them as a substitute for real pricing changes.

cards.title: Exploding Opportunity Urgency
cards.summary: When the value itself decays with time, make the ticking clock explicit and push for fast decisions.
cards.use_when: Offering an arbitrage, market inefficiency, early-access platform, or any opportunity whose returns shrink the longer the buyer waits.
steps: Identify whether the opportunity is time-decaying: market inefficiencies correct over time, so acting sooner matters disproportionately. The source's examples include buying goods on eBay to resell on Amazon, trading crypto, buying a stock, and getting into a new advertising platform before competitors pile in.
Emphasize the decay explicitly in the pitch — the whole point is that every second of delay costs disproportionate gains.

Recognize the same shape in talent markets: 'exploding offers' in competitive hiring environments decrease pay or bonuses each day the candidate waits, forcing a fast decision instead of waiting for a better offer.
Frame your own offer the same way when the mechanism is real, so the prospect decides now rather than trying to time you out.
caveats: Only use this when the opportunity genuinely decays — inventing a clock is the credibility-destroying pattern the source criticizes elsewhere.
Arbitrage windows are examples of decay, not a promise that any specific window will remain open or profitable.
This is a services/information-play pattern; ecommerce uses include early-vendor access or platform-specific ad arbitrage.

cards.title: Bonus Stacks Beat Discounts: Expanding Price-to-Value Discrepancy
cards.summary: Break one offer into named component parts and stack them as bonuses, increasing perceived value rather than cutting price.
cards.use_when: Structuring how a product or service is presented and closing deals where prospects are hesitating on price.
steps: Accept the core premise: a single offer is less valuable than the same offer broken into component parts and stacked as bonuses. Until you enumerate what you actually do, those pieces are unknown to the buyer.

Anchor the price to the core offer, then layer increasingly valuable bonuses so the price-to-value discrepancy grows until it is too big to bear. Classic infomercials sell one knife for $38.95 then pile on 37 knives, sharpeners, pans and guarantees to beat the prospect into submission.

Never discount the main offer to close a deal — it teaches customers that your prices are negotiable, which the source calls terrible. Add bonuses instead: a position of strength and goodwill rather than weakness.
Watch what the infomercial formula does right: it establishes the price, then expands on it until passing feels stupid.
caveats: Bonuses inflate perceived value; the source explicitly notes the implication 'the main thing must be worth more than the bonuses' is psychological bias, not necessarily true.
Do not state bonus values you cannot justify with a real cost or comparison.
Discounting is sometimes the commercially rational choice — this is a strong opinion in the source, not a universal prohibition.

cards.title: Bonus Presentation Rules and the 11-Point Checklist
cards.summary: Name, justify, prove and visualize each bonus, and make its value eclipse the core offer.
cards.use_when: Writing sales copy, webinar slides or a 1-on-1 pitch that includes bonus deliverables.
steps: Always offer bonuses. Give each a special name with a benefit in the title.

For each bonus, tell them: (a) how it relates to their issue, (b) what it is, (c) how you discovered it or what you had to do to create it, (d) how it will make their experience faster, easier or less effort (the value equation).
Provide proof of value — a stat, a past client or personal experience.
Paint a vivid mental image of their life already having used the bonus and reaping the benefits.
Always ascribe a price tag and justify it.
Prefer tools and checklists over additional trainings because effort and time are lower for the buyer, so value is higher.
Make each bonus answer a specific objection in the prospect's mind about why they cannot or will not succeed — the bonus should prove the belief incorrect.
Also address what they will logically realize they need next: solve their next problem before they encounter it.
Let the bonuses' stated value eclipse the core offer; each addition widens the price-to-value gap and subconsciously implies the main offer is worth more.

Add scarcity or urgency to the bonuses themselves to put the technique on steroids — e.g. only buyers of XYZ program get Bonus 1–3, or three tickets left to a $5,000 virtual event included as a bonus, or a $1,000 bonus free only if you buy today.

For what belongs in the bonus vs. the core: pick the 'wow factor' — items you would not want anyone to miss. Short, high-quality assets like checklists or infographics can be worth much more as a bonus than buried inside the core.
caveats: Scarcity on bonuses is quantity-based (never available elsewhere); urgency on bonuses is time-based (only if you buy today). The source flags the subtle difference as worth noting.
The implied 'bonuses prove the core is worth more' logic is psychological positioning, not arithmetic.
Price tags on bonuses should reflect real costs or genuine market comparisons.

cards.title: Sequencing Bonuses in 1-on-1 Selling
cards.summary: Ask for the sale first; use bonuses after a no to match the specific objection, then ask again.
cards.use_when: Closing service or high-ticket deals where prospects raise objections and no group pitch is involved.
steps: When selling one on one, ask for the sale before presenting bonuses.
If they say yes, reveal the additional bonuses after they have signed up. This creates a wow experience and reinforces the decision.

If they say no, present a bonus that matches their perceived obstacle, then ask again. Do not feel weird about asking again: agree with the prospect, add the bonus, and ask whether this is 'fair enough'.
Lean on reciprocity — people have a hard time rejecting it. Add a bonus to accommodate, then another, then another, and they feel almost obligated to buy.

This is why the deliverables from the 'Trim and Stack' exercise are weaponized one at a time at the perfect moment: you were going to provide them anyway, but layering them one at a time increases perceived value.
caveats: The bonus must map to the stated objection or it reads as a random add-on.
The source notes group selling is beyond the scope of this material, so this sequencing is specifically 1-on-1.
Repeated re-asks rely on reciprocity; aggressive use may suit some audiences poorly.

cards.title: Sourcing Bonus Assets and Partner Discounts
cards.summary: Build a vault of one-time-created assets and negotiate adjacent-business bonuses with referral commissions.
cards.use_when: Creating future bonus inventory and building a partner network whose products solve what your customers need next.
steps: Create checklists, tools, swipe files, scripts and templates — anything that takes lots of time and effort to create once but is easy for the buyer to use and can be given away endlessly.
Record every workshop, webinar, event and interview; keep them in a vault to deploy later against a specific perceived obstacle.

Go to adjacent businesses that solve needs your customer will have as a result of starting with you, and negotiate group discounts and a referral commission. You negotiate with the purchasing power of all your customers at once, which is very powerful.

Worked example: a $400 pain-clinic offer can include 1–2 free massages, two chiropractic adjustments ($100), an anti-inflammatory food discount ($50 savings), braces/orthotics discounts ($150), a free training session and pool month ($100), and pharmacy discounts ($100/mo). Stack these across multiple providers — e.g. ten chiropractors each contributing an adjustment — and the bonuses alone can exceed the $400 price.

Then negotiate affiliate commissions on the same intros: the chiropractor pays $100 per new patient, orthotics $100 per referral, the health club $50 per signup or a free membership, the pharmacy $100 per person. On the example, a $400 offer can generate an extra $350 — pure profit on customers you already paid to acquire.

Use high-perceived-value, low-cost vehicles where they fit: information products (extra login only), tickets to virtual events and experiences, and fixed-cost VIP service for a month — which also doubles as an upsell path.
caveats: Partners must not be direct competitors.
The source's $350 extra-profit figure is an illustrative calculation, not a forecast.
These bonuses solve needs triggered by your offer; mismatched partners dilute trust.
In ecommerce, verify the current interface and terms of any affiliate or referral arrangement before committing.

cards.title: Risk Reversal Math: Why Stronger Guarantees Usually Net More
cards.summary: Model the sales lift against the refund increase before rejecting a strong guarantee on emotion.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to strengthen a guarantee and how much refund risk you can absorb.
steps: Start from the premise that risk — that the product does not do what it should for the buyer — is the single greatest objection, so reversing it immediately makes any offer more attractive. The source says Jason Fladlien reported conversion on an offer rising 2–4x simply by changing the quality of the guarantee.

Run the arithmetic before deciding: baseline of 100 sales with 5 refunds (5%) nets 95. With the stronger guarantee, 130 sales and 13 refunds (10%) nets 117 — 1.23x, a 23% increase, all to the bottom line. Doubling the refund rate still produced more net sales.

Note the break-even condition: for a guarantee to be unprofitable, the absolute increase in sales would have to be fully offset by an absolute increase in refunds — e.g. a 5-point absolute sales increase offset by a 5-point absolute refund increase, which would mean the refund rate doubled.
Heed the warning: people who buy only because of a guarantee can be poor customers who may not do the work. Tie the guarantee to the actions they need for success so all parties win.
If your cost of fulfilment is high, use a conditional or anti-guarantee rather than an unconditional one — otherwise you eat both the refund and the cost of delivering.
Always state your guarantee hard, even if you have none: say it boldly and give the reason why.
caveats: The 2–4x conversion figure is attributed to another practitioner's experience, not a universal result.
Consumer entitlement and shifting norms make unconditional guarantees riskier over time.
Guarantee mechanics are jurisdiction-specific for ecommerce — check legal requirements before advertising refund terms.

cards.title: The Four Guarantee Types and How to Choose
cards.summary: Unconditional, conditional, anti- and implied guarantees each fit different ticket sizes, cost structures and business models.
cards.use_when: Designing the risk-reversal clause for an offer, especially deciding between broad refunds and outcome-based terms.
steps: Unconditional: the strongest form — effectively a pay-first trial. It gets many more people to buy but produces some refunds. Example client outcomes: full refund, 50% refund, refund of ad spend plus ancillary costs, you pay for a competitor's program instead, or you return the money plus an additional $1,000.

Conditional: includes terms and conditions and is where you can get very creative. Aim for 'better than money-back' — match their investment with an equal or higher perceived commitment. Build the key success actions into the conditions, with the ideal that 100% of customers qualify but achieve the result and never want the refund. Given the choice between a refund and the promised outcome, the vast majority take the outcome.

Anti-guarantee: explicitly 'all sales are final', owned confidently with a creative reason why that shows a massive exposure or vulnerability the buyer instantly understands. Especially important for consumables or items that massively diminish in value once delivered.

Implied guarantee: any performance-based offer — revshare, profitshare, triggers, ratchets, monetary bonuses. If I do not perform, I do not get paid; if I do a great job, I am very well compensated. Requires transparency in measuring the outcome and trust or control that you will actually be compensated.

Match guarantee breadth to business type: bigger, broader guarantees work better in lower-ticket B2C (many buyers will not bother pursuing a refund); higher ticket and more business-oriented offers should steer toward specific guarantees, with or without refunds and conditions.

Give the guarantee teeth with the conditional formula: 'If you do not get X result in Y time period, we will Z.' Without the 'or what' portion it sounds weak — 'we will get you 20 clients guaranteed' is weak; 'you will get 20 clients in your first 30 days, or we give you your money back plus your advertising spend with us' is strong.
Name the guarantee something memorable rather than 'satisfaction': e.g. 'in 30 days, if you would not jump into shark-infested waters to get our product back, we will return every dollar you paid.'
caveats: The source says the more conditions you add to an unconditional guarantee, the faster it loses its teeth — conditions and unconditional power trade off.
Anti-guarantees need a believable reason why, or they read as mere policy.
Implied guarantees only work where outcomes are measurable and payment is enforceable.
Guarantee language must comply with local consumer law — verify before publishing.

cards.title: Conditional Guarantee Variants: Service, Modified Service and Credit
cards.summary: Use outcome-based guarantees that keep clients working toward the result while limiting your exposure.
cards.use_when: Choosing a conditional guarantee structure for coaching, services or programs where you can keep delivering until the outcome is met.
steps: Service guarantee: keep working for them free until X is achieved. The source calls it his personal favourite — it guarantees the goal while eliminating the time element, so you are never at risk of losing the money. Make it conditional on key success actions: setting up a web page, attending calls, showing up to workouts, weighing in, reporting data. He reports that since advising businesses to use it, not a single client has taken one up; in practice either you happily keep working with a committed client to the result, or it quietly drops because the client is close enough to satisfied and the sales conversation is months in the past.

Modified service guarantee: give another Y-long period of service or access free, where Y is generally at least twice the original duration. This ties a specific duration to your extended involvement instead of being on the hook forever — a good starting point before the all-out service guarantee.
Credit-based guarantee: give back what they paid, but as credit toward any service you offer.

Outsized refund guarantee: double or triple their money back, or a no-strings payment far above the price, attached to a consumption condition. Fladlien's example: spend $X on ads using the course methods and if you do not make money, he buys the store for $25,000. He attributed an extra $3M in sales to it on a $2,997 course and only paid out 10 of the $25,000 refunds. This fits high-margin offers and situations where a lot must be done by the buyer and, if done, results are highly likely.
caveats: Outsized refund guarantees depend on high margins and a genuinely low chance of failure when conditions are met; the $25,000 payout is a case study, not a template for your economics.
The 'nobody claims the service guarantee' observation is the source's experience, not a statistical expectation.
Consumption conditions should reflect actions genuinely required for success, not gimmicks designed to disqualify buyers.

cards.title: Stacking Guarantees for Compounded Risk Reversal
cards.summary: Layer different guarantee types to remove risk sequentially and future-pace the buyer toward the outcome.
cards.use_when: Building a premium offer where a single guarantee is not enough to overcome hesitation.
steps: Layer an unconditional guarantee on top of a conditional one — e.g. a 30-day no-questions-asked refund plus a conditional triple-your-money-back 90-day guarantee.

Stack two conditional guarantees around sequential outcomes: you will make $10,000 by 60 days and $30,000 by 90 days, provided you do things 1, 2 and 3. Spelling out the conditional timeline future-paces the prospect into an outcome they now believe is far more likely.
Treat stacking as evidence you are serious about client results and convinced they will get them — it shifts risk from the buyer back onto you.
caveats: Stacked guarantees multiply your worst-case exposure; model the refund arithmetic from the risk-reversal math card before committing.
Future-pacing with specific dollar milestones sets expectations you must be prepared to honour.

cards.title: Crafting and Delivering an Unconditional Refund Guarantee
cards.summary: Pitch the strongest refund guarantee by removing the decision from today and promising to keep only happy money.
cards.use_when: Writing or delivering the guarantee portion of a webinar, sales page or closing conversation for a lower-ticket B2C offer.
steps: Remove the immediate yes/no: 'I am not asking you to decide yes or no today — I am asking you to make a fully informed decision.' Use the house analogy: you do not buy a house without looking inside, so get inside the program, verify the claims, and decide then.

Echo the source's phrasing: 'whether it is 29 minutes or 29 days from now — if you ain't happy, I ain't happy.' For any reason whatsoever, they can get the money back by emailing support with a simple request.
Back the promise with concrete support metrics if you have them — the original script cited average response times of 61 minutes over a 24/7 period.

Use a satisfaction-based guarantee with a best-case/worst-case close. Weight-loss program example: 'best case you get the body of your dreams; worst case you tell me I suck, I write you a check, and you get six weeks of free training. Both options are risk free — but the only thing guaranteed not to help you is walking out today.' He reports two people took him up on it out of 4,000 sales over three and a half years.

If you use satisfaction-based refunds, be genuinely good at fulfilment — the source credits the guarantee with a lot of closed deals but warns the model is riskier as ticket size and fulfilment cost rise.
caveats: Satisfaction/no-questions-asked is the highest form of guarantee because the buyer could ask for a refund even when you did everything right — the source says this works much better in lower-ticket situations.
His 2-in-4,000 refund rate is an example from his own business, not a benchmark.
Do not emit support response-time claims you cannot substantiate.

cards.title: Strengthening a Guarantee Through Naming and Wording
cards.summary: Give the guarantee a vivid, benefit-laden name and lead with the reason why, so it does not read as boilerplate.
cards.use_when: Finalising the wording and branding of a guarantee for sales copy or checkout messaging.
steps: Replace 'vanilla' terms like 'satisfaction' with a stronger, more concrete description.
Generic example to avoid: '30 Day Money Back Satisfaction Guarantee'.
Good creative imagery: 'In 30 days, if you would not jump into shark-infested waters to get our product back, we will return every dollar you paid.'
Even stronger: the source's 'Club a Baby Seal Guarantee' — after 30 days of using the services, if you would not club a baby seal to stay on as a customer, you do not pay a penny.
Always name the guarantee and state it boldly, with the reason why, even if you choose not to offer one.
caveats: The source's extreme imagery examples are intentionally provocative; tone must fit your brand and audience.
Verify advertising and refund-wording compliance for your market before publishing the named guarantee.

In other words, one fifth of the prospects are willing to pay five times the price (or more). In the example, I might have ten people willing to pay $500, but two of them willing to pay $5000. So, I would make more, have lower costs (more profits), provide more value, and increase the demand in the remaining prospect base by selling fewer units. Think about how exclusive scenario one vs scenario two would feel. Think about all the people who would want to purchase, but would not be able to. Would this increase or decrease their desire? It would increase it, of course. On top of that, if people see that others who ‘were able to get in’ are loving it, it would further increase their desire. And the next time, they would act with more urgency, and be willing to pay more for the same thing than they originally did. So now, in the aftermath of our second scenario, we still have eight people who have unsatisfied desire. This increases their desire further. And to boot, we now have new prospects who weren't in the original pool who now want what we have.

 The next time we promote scenario two, we then open three spots at the same price and sell them all (still leaving some prospects with pent up demand!). This is a continuous theme. Conversely, if we were to promote scenario one again (the $500 price point), we would probably sell fewer slots the second time around. Why? We have no pent up demand. All desire has been satisfied. When you “pull the trigger too early,” each successive instance we promote, we sell even fewer. Eventually, we run out of sufficient demand to make even a single sale. This is the sad state many businesses find themselves in always trying to generate more demand to make another quick sale. Hormozi Law: The longer you delay the ask, the bigger the ask you can make. “The longer the runway, the bigger the plane that can take off.” We must endeavor to keep our supply (and satisfaction of desire) under the demand that we are able to generate. This maximizes profits and keeps desire ravenous in our customer base. This is the real key to never going hungry. Summary Points The reason I titled this sub-section “Delicate Dance of Desire” is that supply and demand are inversely correlated (in theory). If you satisfy zero desire (provide zero supply), you will not make money, and eventually leave people feeling rejected (Note: it takes much longer than you think). Conversely, if you satisfy all the demand, you will kill your golden goose, and not know where your next meal will come from. Mastering supply and demand comes from the elegant dance between the two. If you sleep with your significant other everyday they have less desire than if you haven’t slept with them for a week. We want the ravenous prospect, not merely the aroused. Therefore, understanding the interplay between these variables is key to enhancing your offer and the amount of profits you will make over time. Up to this point, we have covered all the things inside of your offer that can make it immune to price comparison and transform regular services and products into things that people will find a way to pay for. It would follow that the next variable that can make your offer more desirable is how it is presented. In other words, the outside variables that position the product in your prospect’s mind. These forces are often more powerful than your core offer. In this next section Enhancing Your Offer, I will show you how I: 1. Use scarcity to decrease supply to raise prices (and indirectly increase demand through perceived exclusiveness) 2. Use urgency to increase demand by decreasing the action threshold of a prospect. 3. Use bonuses to increase demand (and increase perceived exclusivity). 4. Use guarantees to increase demand by reversing risk. 5. Use names to re-stimulate demand and expand awareness of my offer to my target audience. I will define each, then give you examples of how to use them. We will use all these variables to enhance our offer and shift the demand curve in our favor, leaving our customers always wanting for more. We will start by tactically stimulating “fear of missing out” aka FOMO through scarcity. 12 S ENHANCING THE OFFER: SCARCITY “Sold out.” carcity is one of the most powerful and least understood forces to unlock unlimited pricing power. If you want to learn how to sell air for millions of dollars, then pay attention. The reason an authority (like a doctor), a celebrity (like Oprah), or a celebrity authority (like Dr.Oz or Dr.Phil) can charge egregious rates is because of implied demand. People assume that there is a lot of demand for their time, and, therefore, not a big supply of it. As a result, it must be expensive. That being said, it’s hard for most businesses to understand what it’s really like to have an uneven supply-demand curve until you’ve experienced it. I’m going to try and walk you through what it felt like for me the first time I experienced it in order to give you a taste of the power. When I got into this world of acquisition, I saw mentors of mine selling days of time for $50,000+. My mind was blown for two reasons. First, because I didn’t understand how they could make so much money for a single day. Second, because I didn’t understand who in their right mind was buying it. Over time, I learned. I’ll start with the buyer. If I have a rare problem, and I must solve this problem for my own pursuit of happiness, it will consume all of my attention. By the nature of my problem being specialized, there will be very few people who can solve it. This means there is not a large supply of solvers. In many cases, I will perceive only one possible “solver” (Supply = 1). Real Life Value Case Study There are many people who can solve the problem: how do I make $10,000 per month? But far fewer who can solve: How can I add $5M in profit without adding any extra product lines to my business? (This was a real project that took me 60min and resulted in exactly $5M in bottom line profit by slightly altering the pricing model of the business). You could say the business owner was… “very happy” with the result of the engagement. Beyond that, if solving this problem speeds up my achievement of a goal by a year or two, or immediately results in me making hundreds of thousands of dollars, or millions of dollars, that solution becomes far more valuable, does it not? Of course it does. And so, it would follow, if I can pay someone $50,000 for a day of their time, and see an increase of $500,000 per month in revenue within three months because of the insights and strategies revealed, that would be a helluva return on investment, right? So there are two components to the value: first, how rare the sources are; second, the actual value being provided. The value and rarity compound to create some truly breathtaking profits. Specialized consultants are paid millions of dollars to solve problems worth tens of millions to clients. The client pays for all the experience and expertise the expert has and avoids the cost of errors (time and money). In short, they skip the bad stuff and go straight to the good stuff more quickly and for less money than it would cost to figure it out on their own . . . a beautiful economic exchange. I personally experienced this for the first time when I had two different people offer me $50,000 for a day of my time after speaking at an event. They were scaling an education business in a niche (not too dissimilar from my own) and could not get past the $1M per month mark. As someone who was doing $1M per week in the same business type (at the time), I was a very specific type of person with the keys to their problem. So what happened, you ask? Drum roll . . . I didn’t accept their offers. Why? Because I was making more than $50,000 per day in profit from my business and didn’t want the distraction. Author Note: It was years later that I started Acquisition.com to help these very people. But instead of charging a day rate, I simply become an equity holder in the company to completely align interests for short and long term (and so I can see the implementations through). And as my time is limited by the laws of physics, for everyone else below that $3M-$10M per year mark, I make all these materials for free :) After the event concluded and I was speaking with Leila, I realized how I had somehow become ‘one of those people I had always wondered about’. It was a very surreal experience for me. I finally understood how premium prices were truly made . . . simple supply and demand. There is little that substitutes for incredible demand. You can try and fake it, but there is a special type of “0 fucks given” vibe that’s hard to replicate when you truly do not need a person’s money (or even want it). That’s how these guys can charge so much . . . because they don’t need it. The person who needs the exchange less always has the upper hand. I always try to remember that. It’s one of the negotiating and pricing principles that has best served me in my life. “But Alex, how are you going to show me how to use scarcity to increase the amount of people who want my offer when currently no one does?” Great question. Let’s attack some real-world, in-the-trenches strategies to reliably create scarcity . Creating Scarcity When there’s a fixed supply or quantity of products or services that are available for purchase it creates “scarcity” or a “fear of missing out.” It increases the need to take action, and by extension, purchase your offer. This is where you publicly share that you are only giving away X amount of products or can only handle Y new clients. For example, if a musician drops a limited edition hoodie and says he only made 100 and they will never be made again, are you more or less likely to buy it than one that is always available? More likely, naturally. The idea that you can never get it again makes it more desirable. This is an example of scarcity. It is the fear of missing out on something. It pulls on our psychological fear of loss to get us to take action. Humans are far more motivated to take action to hoard a scarce resource than they are to act on something that could help them. Fear of loss is stronger than desire for gain. We will wield this psychological lever to get your clients to buy in a frenzy, all at once, until you are sold out. Three Types of Scarcity 1. Limited Supply of Seats/Slots: in general or over X period of time. 2. Limited Supply of Bonuses 3. Never available again. But how do you use this properly without being phony? I’ll try and give you some real world examples Physical Products Having limited releases is a tried and true method of using this psychological bias to your advantage. You can have limited releases for flavors, colors, designs, sizes, etc. “This month, we are releasing 100 boxes of mint chocolate cookie flavored protein bars.” Important point: to properly utilize this method you should always sell out. Here’s why: it’s better to sell out consistently than over order and fail at creating that scarcity. This method stacks in effectiveness if it is done repeatedly over time (just not too often). Once a month seems to be the sweet spot for most of the companies that I know who do this with regularity. Second Important Note: When using this tactic, you must also let everyone know that you sold out. That is part of what makes it work so well. This way, even people who were on the fence, when they see that it was sold out, it gives social proof that other people thought it was worth it. And now that the choice has been made for them, they desire it more because there is no way they can get it. So the next time you make the offer they will be far more likely to take you up on it. Fun fact: Chanel, a brand that has maintained insane margins and pricing for over a century, is a master of scarcity. They send only 1-2 of each piece to each store so every store has a different selection and every item is the last or second to last item in stock. This allows them to price far above market and turn buying impulses into purchases. Services With services, especially if you want to consistently get customers, it can be a little trickier to use scarcity. But I will show you a few simple ways to employ scarcity ethically to increase your take rates on offers. These all have similar elements with very slight tweaks. I'm enumerating these because one of these might mentally fit your business model more than others. 1. Total Business Cap - Only accepting….X Clients. Only accepting X clients at this level of service (on-going). This puts a cap on how many clients you service but also keeps them in it. You create a waiting list for new prospects. The moment the door opens, they jump right in and price resistance disappears. Periodically, you can increase capacity by 10-20% then cap it again. This works well for your highest tiers or service levels. a) This is like saying “My agency only will service twenty-five customers total. Period.” Over time you can increase your prices and squeeze the lower performing accounts out and bring in new more profitable accounts, or, you can periodically ‘open slots’ as your capacity allows (always leaving some demand unmet). 2. Growth Rate Cap - Only accepting X clients per week (on-going) “We only accept 5 new clients per week and we already have the first 3 spots taken. I have 6 more calls this week, so you can take the spot or one of my next calls and you can wait until we reopen.” I have used this method since the beginning of my business. I always knew what my capacity was per week, and simply chose to let our prospects know how many openings we had left. This banks on the fact that you can only handle a certain amount of new clients anyways, on a regular basis, so you might as well let them know it. 3. Cohort Cap - Only accepting….X clients per class or cohort. Similar to the above, except done on whatever cadence you desire. Only accepting X amount per class or cohort over a given period is another way of thinking about it. Imagine you only start clients monthly or quarterly. This helps you get some cadences in place in your business operationally while also allowing your sales team some legitimate scarcity. Example: “We take on 100 clients 4 times a year. We open the doors then close them.” Etc. Pro Tip - Provide Limited Access For Higher Ticket Services These scarcity tactics work especially well for higher ticket upsells. If you want to create one off workshops, trainings, events, seminars, consulting, etc. These are things that by their nature take time and provide more access. Paring them with clear scarcity or fixed amounts, seats, or spots will rapidly drive up the demand. But always remember have less spots available than you think you can sell . . . so that when you want to do it again in the future, everyone will remember you sold out . . . fast. This is a compounding strategy that increases in effectiveness over time. One of the few in the marketing arsenal. Let me give you a real example of scarcity to enhance the value of a free lead magnet. If I were to tell you right now that I have a checklist that you can download for free that has all these materials for you in this book in bulleted format, you might be inclined to put this book down and go there to download it now. But, if I told you I have it set so that every week the page only allows twenty new people to download it, you’d be far more likely to go see if you can grab it. And even more so if when you try it, you see that it has already run out for the week. Result? You join a list that notifies you the next time twenty more checklists become available for download. What happens next? When you get that notification, you’ll hit the link on your phone and go to the page because you don’t want to miss out again. By employing scarcity, we make what would otherwise be a “neat free download” into a desirable thing not everyone has access to. You also, by extension, would be far more likely to consume it when you do get your hands on it . . . all because of how we controlled supply. Cool, right? Honest Scarcity (The Most Ethical Scarcity) The easiest scarcity strategy is honesty. Wait, what? Let me explain. I'm sure right now, you probably couldn't handle 1,000 clients tomorrow right? But how many could you handle? 5? 10? 25? Well, you might as well define a number that you are willing to take on in a given time period, then advertise that. Simply letting people know that you are three-fourths of the way to capacity this week will move people over the edge to buying from you. Or letting people know that you are 81% to capacity in your total business, will make people more likely to sign up with you “before they lose the chance.” Scarcity also implies within it, social proof. If you are 81% to capacity then a decent amount of people made the decision to work with you, and the closer you get to your arbitrary fullness, the faster the spots will disappear. But only you get to draw where that line is “full.” Neat right? Summary Points Employ one or multiple methods of scarcity in your business. You will drive a faster purchasing decision from your prospects, and at higher prices. Just let them know your limits and let psychology do the rest. Now that we’ve covered some of my favorite scarcity tactics that you can use year round, what else could you do to increase demand without changing anything about your offer? Increase urgency. We will cover that next. Pro Tip - Extreme Scarcity If you don’t hate money, sell a very limited supply of 1-on-1 access. You can do that via any of the mediums described in “Delivery Cube.” Direct message access. Email Access. Phone access. Voice memo access. Zoom access. Etc. There are lots of ways you can do this. But I promise you this - if you want to immediately make a lot of money, create a very exclusive service level based on access to you (yes, unscalable), that you cap at a tiny number. Price it very high. Then, tell people. You will make more money than you thought possible. These also tend to be some of the best clients. And limit your delivery to something that you don’t hate. For me, I hate emails and messages but dont mind zoom calls. Make it work for your working style. The cream of the crop (the 1% of 1% will adjust and take action). Pro Tip - Once You’re Out, You Can Never Come Back You can create scarcity by also capping your service level and saying that if they leave than can never return. This type of scarcity makes people think extra hard about leaving. I started doing this with my gyms early on. Then I was in a mastermind that employed this. Then I started using it in my higher level of Gym Lords. This works best with small groups (like the above example). As groups become much bigger, the tactic loses some teeth (speaking from experience). 13 S ENHANCING THE OFFER: URGENCY “Deadlines. Drive. Decisions.” — ME carcity is a function of quantity. Urgency is a function of time. This is where you only limit when people can sign up, rather than how many. Having a defined deadline or cut off for a purchase or action to occur creates urgency. Frequently, scarcity and urgency are used together, but I will separate them out for you to illustrate the concepts. I’m going to show you my four favorite ways of using urgency on a consistent basis, ethically: 1) Rolling Cohorts, 2) Rolling Seasonal Urgency, and 3) Promotional or Pricing Urgency 4) Exploding Opportunity. They will employ urgency in your business without being phony. My favorite way of doing this is having cohorts of clients start on a regular cadence. This has the added operational benefit of helping you create a choreographed onboarding experience for new clients. As you scale, this will become increasingly important. 1) Cohort-Based Rolling Urgency For example, if you start clients every week (even in unlimited amounts), you can say: “If you sign up today, I can get you in with our next group that kicks off on Monday, otherwise you’ll have to wait until our next kickoff date.” If you wanted to juice it up a little bit, you could say: “I actually had a client who signed up a few weeks ago drop out, so I have an opening for our next cohort that kicks off on Monday. If you are pretty sure you’re gonna do this sooner or later, might as well get in on it now so you can start reaping the rewards sooner rather than paying the same and waiting.” Those two tweaks above have pushed so many sales over the edge by just reminding a potential customer that if they sign up, they will be starting on Monday, and if they do not, they will have to wait a week. It’s small things like this that nudge people to take the action they know they should take anyways. Obviously the less frequently you kick off new customers, the more powerful this is. For example, if you only start clients two times a year, people will be very inclined to sign up, especially as the date approaches. Even starting new clients every other week can confer this urgency nudge. What if I lose sales by turning business away? Just like guarantees, there is always a fear that you will make less money by employing this strategy. We are afraid that we will lose sales we would have otherwise made. Every experienced marketer on the planet will tell you - it is a fear, and it is unfounded. The biggest sales on a week long campaign or launch happen in the last 4 hours of the last day (up to 50-60%). That means that the last 3% of the time allotted creates 50-60% of the sales...that’s completely illogical, but also unmistakably human. So, just like a guarantee, you will make more money from the many people who decided to take action than people who actually missed out because in reality, those people were never going to buy (heck, they didn't even buy when they had their fee to the fire, so why would they without?) Good to remember. What to do if you just started a cohort and someone wants to buy…. You have two options: 1) you can offer them a speedy personalized onboarding to get them up to speed as a “bonus” for signing up today and still get them in. Or, my preference, 2) You can explain to them that since the next group starts in a little, they will have the advantage of having more time to review the materials, talk to their employees (for b2b products) or family members ( for b2c products). On top of that, they can have a more extended payment plan that you can only make available to them since the start date is so far out . . . an advantage that most clients do not get. In the end, remember, you always have the advantage because you are the one who calls the shots. 2) Rolling Seasonal Urgency In a digital setting, having actual sign up date countdowns is very useful. But make sure they are real. If they aren’t, you’ll lose credibility and just look like every other wannabe marketer. This is very common with internet businesses that use “launch” models. I personally love having the dates that I am running a promotion through on my landing pages and in my copy. I want it to be visible everywhere. The nice thing is that you can always fire up another ad campaign and a new landing page with new dates and be right as rain. You will see your conversions go through the roof, and it takes maybe five minutes of editing — well worth the time investment. Example: Our New Year Promotion ends Jan 30! Next Month: Our Valentines Lovers Promo Ends Feb 30! Next Month: Our Sexy By Spring Special Ends March 31! Next Month: Our Fools in Love April Promo Ends April 30! The actual promotion may be the same, but naming it something different “by season” gives you a “real” differentiator that gives you a start and a finish. Deadlines drive decisions. By simply having these, you can point to them and let human beings push themselves over the edge so as not to miss out. Pro Tip - Local Businesses: This is my number one strategy for local businesses. They must vary their marketing more frequently than national advertisers. Putting a new wrapper with a date on the same core service gives you urgency and novelty that will consistently outperform the “same old” campaigns. 3) Pricing or Bonus-Based Urgency This is another way of creating urgency using your actual offer or promotion/pricing structure as the thing they could miss out on (kind of brilliant!). It allows businesses that sell clients year round to still use urgency. For example, “Yes, let’s get you started today so you can take advantage of the discount you came in for. I’m not sure how long we will be running it as we change them every 4 weeks or so, and this is one of the better ones we have run in a while.” This creates some fear of missing out on the promotion (or discount or bonuses), rather than your actual service. It would be a lie to say that if you own a roofing business you won’t service them if they buy after the date. But, if you talk specifically about the promotion you can often elicit the same urgency on buying in the prospect while maintaining your integrity — win-win. You can interchange a pricing promotion, discount, or added bonuses like free install or free onboarding or an extra workshop (valued at $1,000) if they buy now. These are all things you can swap around your core offer to create urgency. Pro Tip - Clean Your Pipeline With Every Price Change: If you ever really are planning on raising your prices (hopefully soon if you are reading this book!) then you can always clean out your pipeline by letting people know “The price is going up! So get in now!” Never raise your prices without letting people know. It shows a position of strength and will give you a nice little influx of cash from the people in the pipeline who were on the fence. 4) Exploding Opportunity On occasion you will be exposing the prospect to an arbitrage opportunity. The opportunity itself has a ticking time clock, as all great opportunities do. Every second someone delays, they miss out on disproportionate gains. Example: If I was explaining an arbitrage opportunity between buying products on ebay and selling them on amazon, this market inefficiency would over time correct itself. The sooner someone acts the better it will be for them. This could be true for selling someone on the opportunity of trading crypto currencies, buying a stock, getting into a new platform to advertise before competitors jump on the bandwagon. Highly competitive job environments often get job offers that are “exploding offers” everyday they wait to take the job, their pay or bonuses decrease. This forces prospects to make fast decisions rather than try and “wait it out” to see if they get a better offer. All of these examples show opportunities that decay with time, so if you find yourself in front of an opportunity like this, make sure to emphasize it! Summary Points Adding a deadline and incorporating one or multiple forms of urgency will get more people to take action than would otherwise. I have employed all four of these methods with great effectiveness. I suggest you do the same. Next up….Bonuses! Free Gift #7: Bonus Tutorial: How to Ethically Use Scarcity & Urgency If you want to walk through some live (ethical) examples of scarcity & urgency with me, go to Acquisition.com/training/offers and select “Scarcity & Urgency” to watch a short video tutorial. You’ll also be able to grab my Scarcity Urgency Checklist I use when creating offers. As always, it’s absolutely free. Enjoy. 14 I ENHANCING THE OFFER: BONUSES “It’s all gravy baby” — PLAY ON AN OLD ENGLISH SAYING. have to give special thanks to Jason Fladlien for my renewed appreciation for bonuses. They are so powerful that they earned an entire chapter. In this chapter, I’m going to cover: what to offer, how to pick them, how to value them, how to present them, how to price them. The main point I want you to take away from this is that a single offer is less valuable than the same offer broken into its component parts and stacked as bonuses (see image). The entirety of our offer we came up with at the end of the last section. This section is about how to present those pieces in what order. For example, I may in fact do lots of things in my service, but until I enumerate them, they are unknown. This is why every infomercial of all time continues on with “but wait….there’s more!” They would not use these techniques unless they were effective, as every second of air time costs money and must be justified with ROI. You’ll also notice that if you watch those old infomercials, they would sell one knife for $38.95 then include 37 other knives, sharpeners, pans, and guarantees to beat the prospect into submission. They establish the price, then they expand upon it until you feel it’s such a good deal it would be stupid to pass it up. The reason this works is we are increasing the prospect’s price-to-value discrepancy by increasing the value delivered instead of cutting the price. We anchor the price we tell them to the core offer. Then with each increasingly valuable bonus, that discrepancy grows wider and wider until it's too big to bear and we snap the rubber band in their mind that is holding their wallet in their pocket. We are now going to present that “stack” of deliverables that we assembled earlier in a way that makes them irresistible. Pro Tip: Add Bonuses Instead of Discounting Whenever Possible on Core Offers Whenever trying to close a deal, never discount the main offer. It teaches your customers that your prices are negotiable (which is terrible). Adding bonuses to increase value to close the deal is far superior to cutting prices. It puts you in a position of strength and goodwill rather than weakness. Presenting Bonuses 1-on-1 vs Group Selling There are key differences between pitching to a group versus a single person. Group selling is beyond the scope of this book. But I want to at least address when a bonus would be brought up in a 1-1 selling scenario. When selling one on one, you ask for the sale first, before offering the bonuses. If they say yes, then after they have signed up, you let them know the additional bonuses they're going to get. This creates a wow experience and reinforces their decision to buy. On the other hand, if the person does not buy after the first ask, then you present a bonus that matches their perceived obstacle, then ask again. Don’t feel weird about asking again. You simply agree with the prospect, add the bonus, and ask if this consolation was “Fair enough.” People have a hard time rejecting reciprocity, so adding a bonus to accommodate, then another, then another, and people will feel almost obligated to buy from you. If you recall from our “Trim and Stack” chapter, each of those deliverables is now being weaponized and presented at the perfect time. We’re going to provide all these bonuses to them anyways, but it increases the perception of our offer’s value by layering these bonuses one at a time. Bonus Bullets That being said, there are a few key things to remember when offering bonuses: 1. Always offer them (you can use the bulleted bundle we came up with at the end of Section III) 2. Give them a special name that has a benefit in the title 3. Tell them: a) How it relates to their issue b) What it is c) How you discovered it, or what you had to do to create it d) How it will specifically improve their lives or make their experience i) Faster, easier or less effort/sacrifice (value equation) 4. Provide some proof (this can be a stat, a past client, or personal experience) to prove that this thing is valuable 5. Paint a vivid mental image of what their life will be like assuming they have already used it and are experiencing the benefits 6. Always ascribe a price tag to them and justify it 7. Tools & checklists are better than additional trainings (as the effort & time are lower with the former, so the value is higher. The value equation still reigns supreme). 8. They should each address a specific concern/obstacle in the prospects mind about why they can’t or won’t be successful (bonus should prove their belief incorrect) 9. This can also be what they would logically realize they will need next. You want to solve their next problem before they even encounter it. 10. The value of the bonuses should eclipse the value of the core offer. Psychologically as you continue to add offers, it continues to expand the price to value discrepancy. Jason Fladlien, who I referenced earlier, once stated that he had seen the conversion on an offer 2-4x simply by changing the quality of the guarantee. It’s that important. From an overarching perspective there are four types of guarantees: 1. Unconditional 2. Conditional 3. Anti-Guarantee 4. Implied Guarantees. You must always hit your guarantee hard, even if you don't have one. Say it boldly and give the reason why. But won’t people take advantage of a crazy guarantee? Sometimes, but not usually. That being said, you must understand the math. If you close 130 percent as many people, and your refund percentage doubles from 5 percent to 10 percent, you’ve still made 1.23x the money, or 23 percent more, and that all goes to the bottom line. Ex: 100 sales, 5 refunds (5%) = 95 Net Sales Guarantee Offer 130 sales, 13 refunds (10%)= 117 Net sales 117/95 = 1.23x (23% increase) Don't be emotional, just do the math. For a guarantee to not be worth it, the increase in sales would have to be 100 percent offset by people who refunded. So an absolute increase in sales of 5 percent would need to be offset by an absolute increase in refunds of 5 percent (but that might be a doubling of refunds, which is unlikely). So, for the most part, the stronger the guarantee, the higher the net increase in total purchases, even if the refund rate increases alongside it. Warning: While guarantees can be effective sellers, people who buy because of guarantees can become very shitty customers. A person who only buys because of a guarantee is a person who may not be willing to put in the work necessary to see success with your product or service. In a world where you want to reverse risk and get customers the best outcome possible, tying your guarantee to the things they need to do to be successful can help all parties. Pro Tip: High Cost Services Warning If you have a tremendous amount of cost associated with your product or service, you will likely want to employ a conditional guarantee or an ANTI guarantee, as you will have to eat the cost of the refund AND the cost of fulfilling. Types of Guarantees What makes a guarantee have power is a conditional statement: If you do not get X result in Y time period, we will Z. To give a guarantee teeth you have to decide what you’ll do if they don’t get the result. Without the “or what” portion of the guarantee, it sounds weak and diluted. Note: This is what most marketers do. Bad Example: We will get you 20 clients guaranteed. Better example: You will get 20 clients in your first 30 days, or we give you your money back + your advertising dollars spent with us. This is a simple, but strong guarantee. Here are the four types of guarantees. I’ll go over them in theory then we will apply them. 1) Unconditional Guarantees As I stated earlier, there are unconditional, conditional, and “anti-” guarantees. Unconditional are the strongest guarantees. They're basically a trial where they pay first then see if they like it. This gets a LOT more people to buy, but you will have some people refund, especially as consumer culture continues to shift towards entitlement and zero accountability. 2) Conditional Guarantees Conditional guarantees include “terms and conditions” to the guarantee. These are the ones you can get VERY creative on. In general, you want these to be “better than money back” guarantees. Because if they are going to make an investment, you want to match their investment psychologically with an equal or higher perceived commitment. These also can have a very powerful effect on getting clients results. If you know the key actions someone must take in order to be successful, make those part of the conditional guarantee. In a perfect world, 100% of your customers would qualify for a conditional guarantee, but will have achieved their result, and therefore will not want to take it. That is an ideal we can all aspire towards. And just fyi - if given the option of getting a refund or getting the outcome they were promised the vast majority of people will take the outcome. 3) Anti-Guarantees Anti-guarantees are when you explicitly state “all sales are final.” You will want to own this position. You must come up with a creative “reason why” the sales are final. Typically, you’ll want to show a massive exposure or vulnerability on your part that a consumer could immediately understand and think “Yes, that makes sense.” These types of guarantees are especially important with items that are consumable or massively diminish in value once given. 4) Implied Guarantees Implied guarantees are any offer that is a performance-based offer. This comes in many different forms. Revshare, profitshare, triggers, ratchets, monetary bonuses, etc are all examples. The end all concept is the same, if I don't perform, I don’t get paid. Unique to this particular structure, it also confers the upside of “If I do a great job, I will be very well compensated.” These only work in situations where you have transparency for measuring the outcome and trust (or control) that you will get compensated when you do perform. Stacking Guarantees An experienced salesman understands that, like bonuses, you can actually stack guarantees. For example, you could give an unconditional 30 day no questions asked guarantee then on top of that give a conditional triple your money back 90 day guarantee. That would be an example of stacking an unconditional with a conditional guarantee. You can also stack two conditional guarantees around different (or sequential) outcomes. For example, you’ll make $10,000 by 60 days, $30,000 by 90 days as long as you do thing 1, 2, and 3. This future paces the prospect into an outcome they now believe is far more likely (since you will be deliberately spelling it out in a conditional guarantee with a timeline for achievement). Doing this shows the prospect you are serious about getting them results and convinced that they will achieve what they want. This shifts the burden of risk back from them onto us...a very powerful strategy.
